## The cart has two answers {.center .cart-hook}

**Motion predicts 4 meters.** A sensor reads **7 meters**.

Where should a moving cart think it is **right now**?

<div class="cart-choice" role="img" aria-label="Motion guess at 4 meters and sensor reading at 7 meters on a track; the answer is still open."><span>4 m<br><small>motion</small></span><span class="cart-choice-question">Your guess?</span><span>7 m<br><small>sensor</small></span></div>

**Pick a position between them.** We will return to your answer.

## Probability starts with a count

Suppose a student tries **100 practice questions** and answers **77** correctly. These are example numbers for the lesson.

In the bag activity, a clue changed our guess. Here we will count a known group before changing the question.

$$P(\text{correct}) = \frac{\text{correct answers}}{\text{all questions}} = \frac{77}{100} = 0.77 = 77\%$$

The denominator answers: **Which questions are we counting out of?** Here it is all 100 questions.

## Quick check: which group is on the bottom?

We know a question **was a word problem**. We want the chance it was answered correctly.

Should we count out of **100 questions**, **77 correct answers**, or **20 word problems**?

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
**20 word problems.** The known clue selects the group we count inside. Of those 20, 10 were correct.
:::

To restart the count at any point, first ask: **Which group are we looking inside?**

## Focus on the 20 word problems {.dense-diagram auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}

Both circles grow for a closer view. Their areas and shared region keep the same proportions.

Of these **20** word problems, just **10** were answered correctly.

::: {.legacy-diagram}

## Turn that count into a probability {.dense-diagram auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}

$$\frac{10\text{ correct word problems}}{20\text{ word problems}} = 0.50 = 50\%$$

The bar **|** is read “given.” So $P(\text{correct} \mid \text{word problem})$ asks: “What fraction were correct **among the word problems**?”

::: {.legacy-diagram}

<div data-id="circle2" style="position: absolute; left: 716.111px; top: 230.755px; width: 448.490px; height: 448.490px; background: rgba(100, 255, 100, 0.22); border: 4px solid #64ff64; border-radius: 50%;"></div>

<div data-id="circle1" style="position: absolute; left: 80.000px; top: 15.000px; width: 880.000px; height: 880.000px; background: rgba(255, 100, 100, 0.30); border: 4px solid #ff6464; border-radius: 50%;"></div>

<div data-id="label1" style="position: absolute; left: 762px; top: 500px; width: 195px; color: white; font-size: 28px; text-align: center;">10 correct<br>word problems</div>

<div data-id="label2" style="position: absolute; left: 1080px; top: 70px; color: white; font-size: 34px;">$$P(\text{Word Problem})$$</div>



:::
<!-- Slide 5: Understanding Set Space (Part 3 - AND) -->

## The denominator follows the question {auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}

For “correct **given word problem**,” we count out of the 20 word problems:

$$P(\text{correct} \mid \text{word problem}) = \frac{\text{correct and word problem}}{\text{word problem}} = \frac{10}{20} = 50\%$$

The word after **given** tells us which group goes on the bottom.

## Reverse the question, change the answer {auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}

Now ask: “Of the **77 correct answers**, how many were word problems?”

$$P(\text{word problem} \mid \text{correct}) = \frac{\text{correct and word problem}}{\text{correct answers}} = \frac{10}{77} \approx 13.0\%$$

The overlap is still **10**. The denominator changed from **20** to **77**.

## Find the overlap another way {auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}

Start with the fraction answered correctly, then ask what fraction of those correct answers were word problems:

$$P(\text{correct and word problem}) = P(\text{correct}) \times P(\text{word problem} \mid \text{correct})$$

$$\frac{77}{100} \times \frac{10}{77} = \frac{10}{100}$$

The **77** cancels. We recover the same 10 overlapping questions out of 100.

## Bayes' rule connects the two questions {.compact-slide auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}

We wanted the chance of a correct answer **among word problems**. Use the overlap we just found:

$$P(\text{correct} \mid \text{word problem}) = \frac{P(\text{correct})\,P(\text{word problem} \mid \text{correct})}{P(\text{word problem})}$$

$$\frac{(77/100)(10/77)}{20/100} = \frac{10/100}{20/100} = \frac{10}{20} = 50\%$$

Bayes' rule gives the same answer as counting directly. It is useful when we know the probabilities but cannot see every case in a table.

## The short version so far {.center .rejoin-slide}

**“And”** means the shared cases. Here, that is **10 questions**.

**“Given”** tells us which group to count inside. For word problems, that is **20 questions**.

**10 out of 20 = 50%.** The long formula reaches the same answer.

Keep those three facts as we switch from questions to a moving cart.

## Why would a cart need two guesses?

Imagine a cart moving along a straight track. We want to know where it is now.

1. **Guess from motion:** Using its last known position and speed, we predict the cart is near **4 meters now**. Its speed may have changed.
2. **Guess from a sensor:** A sensor reports about **7 meters**. The sensor may be noisy.

The two guesses disagree. **Which one should pull our final answer more?**

## Two Guesses About One Location {.gaussian-slide auto-animate=true auto-animate-easing="ease-in-out"}

The **green hump** is our motion guess; the **blue hump** is the new sensor reading. The highest point of each hump is its best guess.

The green hump is wider, so it allows more possible locations. The blue hump is narrower, so we have more reason to trust it.

<div class="gaussian-canvas" role="img" aria-label="A broad model prediction and a narrower sensor measurement shown as probability distributions.">
  <div class="probability-baseline"></div>
  <div data-id="model-curve" class="distribution model-distribution" style="left: 120px; width: 760px; height: 380px;"></div>
  <div data-id="sensor-curve" class="distribution sensor-distribution" style="left: 890px; width: 440px; height: 520px; opacity: 1;"></div>
  <div data-id="model-mean" class="mean-line model-mean" style="left: 500px; height: 390px;"></div>
  <div data-id="sensor-mean" class="mean-line sensor-mean" style="left: 1110px; height: 530px;"></div>
  <div data-id="model-label" class="curve-label" style="left: 300px;">Motion guess: about 4 m</div>
  <div data-id="sensor-label" class="curve-label" style="left: 990px;">Sensor: about 7 m</div>
</div>

<div class="gaussian-legend">
  <span><i class="legend-swatch model-swatch"></i> Wider curve = less sure of the location</span>
  <span><i class="legend-swatch sensor-swatch"></i> Narrower curve = more sure of the location</span>
</div>

## A first answer with ordinary algebra

The motion guess is **4 m**. The sensor says **7 m**. The gap between them is **3 m**.

For this example, let the steadier sensor pull us **three quarters of the way** across that gap:

$$4 + 0.75(7-4) = 4 + 2.25 = 6.25\text{ m}$$

The answer is between 4 and 7, and closer to 7. Later we will calculate the 0.75 from how much each source tends to vary.

## Combine the Two Location Guesses {.gaussian-slide auto-animate=true auto-animate-easing="ease-in-out"}

The calculation put our guess at **6.25 m**, between the two readings and closer to the steadier blue one.

The white hump is narrower than either starting hump: using both clues rules out some locations.

<div class="gaussian-canvas" role="img" aria-label="The model prediction moves toward the more precise sensor measurement and becomes a narrower posterior distribution.">

  <div data-id="sensor-curve" class="distribution sensor-distribution" style="left: 890px; width: 440px; height: 520px; opacity: 0.22;"></div>

  <div data-id="sensor-mean" class="mean-line sensor-mean" style="left: 1110px; height: 530px; opacity: 0.22;"></div>
  <div data-id="model-label" class="curve-label posterior-label" style="left: 790px;">Updated guess: about 6.25 m</div>
</div>

## The Four-Step Loop

<div class="kalman-flow" aria-label="Kalman filter cycle: make a prediction, read the sensor, compare confidence, update the guess, then repeat.">
<div class="flow-card fragment fade-up">
<span class="flow-number">1</span>
<h3>Make a guess</h3>
<p>Use the last position and direction of travel to predict what happens next.</p>
</div>
<div class="flow-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</div>
<div class="flow-card fragment fade-up">
<span class="flow-number">2</span>
<h3>Read the sensor</h3>
<p>Get a fresh—but imperfect—observation of where the object is.</p>
</div>
<div class="flow-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</div>
<div class="flow-card fragment fade-up">
<span class="flow-number">3</span>
<h3>Compare confidence</h3>
<p>Ask which source has usually been more dependable.</p>
</div>
<div class="flow-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</div>
<div class="flow-card fragment fade-up">
<span class="flow-number">4</span>
<h3>Update the guess</h3>
<p>Move toward the sensor by the appropriate amount, then repeat.</p>
</div>
</div>

::: {.takeaway-line}
**Predict where the cart is. Read the sensor. Move the guess toward the more dependable reading.**
:::

## Motion Fills the Gaps {.motion-gap-slide}

Sensors give us **snapshots**. The object keeps moving between those snapshots.

<div class="motion-timeline" role="img" aria-label="At zero seconds the sensor sees the object at two meters. At one second there is no reading, so motion predicts three meters. At two seconds the sensor sees 4.2 meters and the estimate is corrected.">
<div class="motion-step observed">
<span class="time-label">0 seconds</span>
<span class="timeline-dot"></span>
<strong>Sensor sees 2.0 m</strong>
<small>Start with an observed position</small>
</div>
<div class="timeline-connector"></div>
<div class="motion-step predicted">
<span class="time-label">1 second</span>
<span class="timeline-dot"></span>
<strong>No new reading</strong>
<small>Motion predicts about 3.0 m</small>
</div>
<div class="timeline-connector"></div>
<div class="motion-step corrected">
<span class="time-label">2 seconds</span>
<span class="timeline-dot"></span>
<strong>Sensor sees 4.2 m</strong>
<small>Use it to correct the prediction</small>
</div>
</div>

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Remember only position

“It was at 2.0 m.” The estimate becomes stale as soon as the object moves.
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
### Remember position and motion

“It was at 2.0 m and moving right.” Now we can make a useful prediction while the sensor is silent.
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway-line}
**Motion carries the estimate forward. The next sensor reading pulls it back toward reality.**
:::

## The “Trust Dial” Controls the Move

<div class="gain-grid">
<div class="gain-card">
<span class="gain-value">Dial near 0</span>
<h3>Mostly trust motion</h3>
<p>The sensor is unreliable, so the guess barely moves toward it.</p>
</div>
<div class="gain-card active-gain">
<span class="gain-value">Dial in the middle</span>
<h3>Blend both</h3>
<p>Both sources have value, so the answer lands between them.</p>
</div>
<div class="gain-card">
<span class="gain-value">Dial near 1</span>
<h3>Mostly trust the sensor</h3>
<p>The reading is dependable, so the guess moves close to it.</p>
</div>
</div>

::: {.plain-language-equation}
**Updated guess** = motion prediction + **some fraction of the gap** toward the sensor
:::

Engineers call that fraction the **Kalman gain**. The filter calculates it from how much each source tends to vary.

## Typical error versus squared spread

A camera might usually miss by about **0.10 m**. We call that a typical error size.

To compare uncertainty in the trust-dial formula, the filter **squares** that size:

$$0.10\text{ m} \times 0.10\text{ m} = 0.01\text{ m}^2$$

If the typical error grows to **1.50 m**, its square is **2.25 m²**. A big error produces a much bigger spread number.

**Meters squared measures spread here.** It is not another position along the track.

## How the Filter Sets the Trust Dial {#kalman-gain-math .compact-slide}

```{=html}
<div class="gain-math-slide">
<div class="gain-main-equation"><span>Sensor's share of the gap</span><strong>K = P⁻ ÷ (P⁻ + R)</strong><small>P⁻ is spread in the motion guess. R is spread in the sensor reading. They use the same units: m².</small></div>
<div class="gain-definition-row"><div><strong>P⁻</strong><span>Motion spread</span><small>More wheel slip raises this number.</small></div><div><strong>R</strong><span>Sensor spread</span><small>More sensor noise raises this number.</small></div><div><strong>K</strong><span>Sensor influence</span><small>Near 0: little pull. Near 1: strong pull.</small></div></div>
<div class="gain-example reliable"><h3>Our 4 m versus 7 m example</h3><p>Suppose motion spread is 0.03 m² and sensor spread is 0.01 m².</p><strong>K = 0.03 ÷ (0.03 + 0.01) = 0.75</strong><p>Updated position = 4 + 0.75 × (7 − 4) = <strong>6.25 m</strong></p></div>
<div class="gain-math-caption">If sensor spread R grows, K shrinks and the guess moves less. If motion spread P⁻ grows, K rises and the sensor gets more say.</div>
</div>
```

## Three numbers to watch in the cart demo {.center .rejoin-slide}

**Motion guess:** where the cart should be from its movement.

**Sensor reading:** where the sensor says it is.

**Updated guess:** a point between them. It moves toward the sensor by **K × the gap**.

First watch these three markers. Then change **K** and see which way the updated guess moves.

<div class="belief-key-row estimate-key"><i></i><strong>Updated guess</strong><small data-role="estimate-value">6.00 m</small><em data-overflow-for="estimate-marker"></em></div>
<div class="belief-key-row sensor-key"><i></i><strong>Sensor</strong><small data-role="measurement-value">6.00 m</small><em data-overflow-for="sensor-marker"></em></div>
</div>
<div class="belief-panel">
<span class="panel-title">Machine understanding — three competing locations</span>
<div class="belief-track"></div>
<div class="belief-marker prior-marker" data-role="prior-marker" aria-label="Motion guess marker"><span></span></div>
<div class="belief-marker measurement-marker" data-role="sensor-marker" aria-label="Sensor marker"><span></span></div>
<div class="belief-marker estimate-marker" data-role="estimate-marker" aria-label="Updated guess marker"><span></span></div>
</div>
</div>

<div class="kalman-live-math" aria-live="polite">
<div><span>Guess from motion</span><strong>Where wheels predict</strong><small>Motion predicts <b data-role="math-prior">6.00 m</b> at <b data-role="model-speed">0.00 m/s</b></small></div>
<div><span>Sensor reading</span><strong>Where the sensor points</strong><small>Ultrasonic reads <b data-role="math-sensor">6.00 m</b></small></div>
<div><span>Gap between them</span><strong>reading − guess</strong><small>Difference = <b data-role="innovation">0.00 m</b></small></div>
<div><span>Updated guess</span><strong>guess + K × gap</strong><small><b data-role="equation">6.00 + 0.55 × 0.00 = 6.00 m</b></small></div>
</div>

<div class="sim-footer">
<span>Command <strong data-role="drive-status">STOP</strong></span>
<span>Model speed <strong data-role="footer-model-speed">0.00 m/s</strong></span>
<span>Motion spread P⁻ ≈ <strong data-role="prior-variance">0.040 m²</strong></span>
<span>Sensor variance R = <strong data-role="sensor-variance">0.123 m²</strong></span>
<span>Updated spread P ≈ <strong data-role="posterior-variance">0.018 m²</strong></span>
</div>
</div>

## What If Two Sensors Disagree?

Imagine two people estimating where a cart stopped along a straight track.

- One says **4 m**. Their estimates are usually close to the truth.
- The other says **6 m**. Their estimates tend to vary more.

Use a result **between 4 m and 6 m**, closer to the steadier observer. The next demo does this with two sensors.

## Why the Combination Works Better

<div class="comparison-grid">
<div class="comparison-card">
<span class="comparison-icon">Motion only</span>
<h3>It drifts</h3>
<p>Tiny errors accumulate, so the predicted position slowly wanders away.</p>
</div>
<div class="comparison-card">
<span class="comparison-icon">Sensor only</span>
<h3>It jitters</h3>
<p>Individual readings bounce around, even when the object moves smoothly.</p>
</div>
<div class="comparison-card comparison-best">
<span class="comparison-icon">Kalman filter</span>
<h3>It stays smooth and grounded</h3>
<p>Motion fills the gaps; sensors keep the prediction connected to reality.</p>
</div>
</div>

::: {.highlight-box}
A Kalman filter does not claim to know the exact truth. It keeps a **best guess plus an honest measure of confidence**, then improves both whenever new evidence arrives.
:::

## From a straight track to a top-down map {.center .dimension-slide}

The cart moved along a line, so **one number** told us where it was: for example, 6 m along the track.

<div class="dimension-bridge" aria-label="One-dimensional track position becomes a two-dimensional floor position with direction">
<div><strong>On a track</strong><span class="dimension-track"><i></i></span><small>position = distance along the line</small></div>
<div><strong>On a floor</strong><span class="dimension-floor"><i></i></span><small>position = left/right + forward/back</small></div>
</div>

A robot can also turn. The next view looks **down from above** so we can see its position and which way it faces. The same guess → sensor → update loop still applies.

## What to watch in the camera comparison {.center .rejoin-slide}

All four setups follow the **same route**. Each one starts with the same wheel motion and front-camera reading.

The other cameras add more clues. Watch the **cumulative average position error** in each panel: smaller means the guesses have been closer to the real robot.

The displays move quickly. Follow **one number per panel** on the first pass.

## More Cameras Cannot Fix the Same Mistake {#calibration-error-floor .compact-slide}

```{=html}
<div class="calibration-simple">
<p class="calibration-lead">Imagine four cameras built with the <strong>same misplaced zero mark</strong>, like four rulers that all start 0.60 m too far right.</p>
<div class="calibration-simple-grid">
<div><h3>Separate random wobble</h3><p>One camera's readings scatter by about <strong>0.80 m</strong>. Averaging four independent readings cuts that typical wobble to about <strong>0.40 m</strong>.</p></div>
<div><h3>Shared wrong starting point</h3><p>All four cameras are shifted <strong>0.60 m</strong> the same way. Their average is still shifted <strong>0.60 m</strong>.</p></div>
</div>
<p class="calibration-simple-fix">Calibration checks the cameras against a known position and fixes the shared shift.</p>
<p class="calibration-takeaway"><strong>More cameras can calm random wobble. They cannot cancel a mistake they all share.</strong></p>
</div>
```

## What to Remember {.center .conclusion-slide}

```{=html}
<div class="conclusion-wrap">
<p class="conclusion-lead">Our opening cart: motion said <strong>4 m</strong>, the sensor said <strong>7 m</strong>, and our trust dial moved the guess to <strong>6.25 m</strong>.</p>
<div class="conclusion-steps" aria-label="Four ideas from the presentation">
<div><span>1</span><h3>Count</h3><p>Start with what has happened so far.</p></div>
<div><span>2</span><h3>Update</h3><p>Use each new clue to revise the guess.</p></div>
<div><span>3</span><h3>Combine</h3><p>If readings disagree, listen more to the steadier source.</p></div>
<div><span>4</span><h3>Repeat</h3><p>Carry the new guess forward, then check the next reading.</p></div>
</div>
<div class="conclusion-loop"><strong>Predict</strong><i>→</i><strong>Measure</strong><i>→</i><strong>Update</strong><i>→</i><strong>Repeat</strong></div>
<p class="conclusion-caveat">A Kalman filter repeats this loop. <strong>More cameras can reduce random errors; shared mistakes need calibration.</strong></p>
</div>
```
